body.text: Treasurer Jim Chalmers is promising a modest save in the upcoming mid-year budget update but insists he is not talking about a "slash and burn" approach.

One Nation says Labor's low polling is 'untenable'
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has said the PM's job could be at risk after a few bad weeks and declining popularity.
The latest Newspoll yesterday put Angus Taylor as the preferred PM over Anthony Albanese, 42 per cent to 41 per cent. (The margin of error in the poll is 3.3 per cent.)
The poll also put Labor and One Nation at 27 per cent on the primary vote — which is a near-record low for Labor, and also a dip for One Nation.
Joyce suggested the knives could be out.
"You can't go on with polling in the 20s. That's untenable. You're the government. You're not a party in opposition," Joyce said.
"They've thrown Jim Chalmers under a bus, they'll throw Chris Bowen under a bus ... maybe that's not such a bad thing."
"Once they start Stalin-like executing their generals, you know that it's not good for the battle."
Extension of homebirth indemnity insurance 'not simple'
The federal government says it cannot extend an exemption that lets midwives attend private home births without indemnity insurance.

Assistant Health Minister Rebecca White says all nine health ministers, including the Commonwealth, agreed 18 months ago to end the exemption, after an insurance product became available for endorsed midwives.
She says extending it would require changes to laws in every state and territory.

"It's not as simple as asking the federal government to continue an exemption. This is an amendment that would need to be made to the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law, which then also needs to be amended by each state and territory parliament because it's enacted through their jurisdiction. So I just wanted to be really clear that is certainly a reasonable question for people to ask, but that is not a pathway," she said.
Government considering alternatives for homebirth indemnity insurance
The federal government has acknowledged that some women in rural and regional areas may struggle to access private homebirths from January.
An exemption letting midwives attend homebirths without indemnity insurance is ending, as a new insurance product becomes available.
But the product will only be available to endorsed midwives who've undertaken extra training.
Assistant Health Minister Rebecca White says the government is looking into alternative insurance for all other midwives.

"For the small number of women who do choose to have a private homebirth, we understand that in rural and regional areas, there may be difficulty in accessing a private endorsed midwife, but we don't expect it'll be as difficult in metro and urban areas," she said.
Greens hopeful deal close on digital duty of care
Greens leader David Shoebridge is hopeful the week will end with the passage of the digital duty of care legislation.

The bill would put the onus on big tech companies to prevent foreseeable harms online. The government, which needs the Greens to pass the legislation, says it's considering its demand for individuals to be able to sue tech companies if they are harmed.
It's one of the four pieces of legislation the government is hoping to pass this week, alongside changes to the capital gains tax discount, trusts and private health insurance rebates for over 65s.
Shoebridge says some negotiations are going better than others.

"There's a lot of tax bills floating around. That's complicated discussions. We'll continue to talk. But our goal at the end of the day is not to give corporate Australia a big Christmas present," he says.

"The government keeps asking, and we keep telling them the same thing: you exempt all pensioners [from the private health rebate change], and there's a pathway through."I mean, it is a bit frustrating that we've said this now for months, and the government seems to think that there's some alternative solution."
"The government keeps asking, and we keep telling them the same thing: you exempt all pensioners [from the private health rebate change], and there's a pathway through.
"I mean, it is a bit frustrating that we've said this now for months, and the government seems to think that there's some alternative solution."
Greens frustrated no relief in pipeline for struggling Australians
Greens leader David Shoebridge isn't too pleased there doesn't seem to be any cost-of-living relief on the way for Australians doing it tough.
He's accused the government of running an "austerity budget" and repeated his call for Labor to adopt a tax on gas exports.
"We've got a treasurer coming out and saying there's going to be no relief, and in fact looking to have an austerity budget," he says.
"This is the exact wrong time to have an austerity budget, take services and support away from ordinary Australians.

"We know that there are revenue sources the government can tap into: a tax on export gas, getting resource sector to pay its fair share, stopping $16.3b in fossil fuels subsidies to corporate Australia, and that would provide the headroom so that Australians could get a bit of relief."
Chalmers trying to 'soften' the blow for challenging 2027: Wilson
So what did Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson make of Jim Chalmers's economic statement?
Wilson thinks he's trying to "soften the impact" for what is going to be challenging 2027.

"What he's trying to do is front run what is clearly going to be further bad news ... the economic conditions, sadly, are deteriorating because of the economic model the Albanese government's pursued," he says.
Key Event
Coalition, Labor squabble over where to find savings in mid-year budget update
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson wants the government to rein in spending but isn't a fan of the areas it's targeting so far, such as the private health insurance rebate change.
The contentious plan would wind back the rebate Australians aged 65 and older receive, banking $3b over four years to be redirected to other aged care spending.
It's something the Coalition is against. But the government argues if the opposition wants budget repair, it should be in favour of the policy.
Wilson tells ABC Radio National Breakfast it's "false economics" and will increase costs in order to deliver a "short-term win" for the government.

Basically, his argument is the government should instead adopt the Coalition's $31b in savings, which include cutting things like climate and housing funding (something I can't imagine Labor would jump on board with anytime soon).
Chalmers not focused on 'columns or the commentary'
A fair amount of newspaper column inches have been taken up assessing Jim Chalmers's performance as treasurer in recent months.
He insists he's not focused on the noise, which he says is just a response to him pushing through "difficult reforms" such as an overhaul of the capital gains tax discount and negative gearing.
But Chalmers tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast he's always willing to take on feedback.
"I’m not focused on the columns or the commentary or that kind of speculation that you see in parts of our media from time to time," he says.

"I always take feedback on board … I take responsibility for the difficult reforms that we’re pushing through, and I understand we’re doing that at a time when people are under pressure, and that will be reflected in the polls. And that those polls will be reflected in the columns and in the commentary. But that’s not my focus."
Chalmers points the finger at Coalition over demand for savings cuts
A proposed reduction in the private health insurance rebate for older Australians is currently stalled before the Senate.
The government wants to wind back the rebate Australians aged 65 and older receive, banking the $3b over four years to be spent elsewhere in the aged care sector.
But it needs the support of the Coalition or the Greens to get the bill through parliament ... and so far neither have been willing to play ball.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says if the Coalition wants to demand the government undertake budget repair then "they need to actually vote for it".
"They're calling for budget repair at the same time as they vote against budget repair in the Senate. So we have to call that behaviour out," he says.

"Right across the board, we need the parliament to play a responsible role in the fight against inflation. This is an opportunity for the Coalition to put their money where their mouth is and not just call for that budget repair but to actually vote for it."
Key Event
MYEFO won't be a 'slash and burn': Chalmers
Next month's budget update will forecast softer economic growth, higher inflation and higher unemployment than previously expected.

That's the picture Jim Chalmers painted in an economic address to parliament yesterday. The treasurer tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast he wanted to give Australians with a "sense of what we're grappling with" ahead of the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook next month.
Included in that update will be a "modest" net saving. So what does that look like? Chalmers doesn't really want to get into it.
Asked if there are any areas that have been protected from the cuts, Chalmers says it's not going to include "slash and burn" cuts.
"We haven't focused the savings on just one portfolio. There will be a number of savings in the mid-year update," he says.
"These are serious times. They do warrant a substantial response."
Market reaction to Nvidia reinstatement shows global market volatility: Chalmers
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is first up in the ABC Radio National Breakfast hot seat this morning, were he was asked to weigh in on the reinstatement of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang.
Huang was reinstated after he stood down over revelations of extra material affairs, including one with suspected Chinese spy.
Chalmers doesn't really want to weigh into the saga but says the global stock market's reaction has been "extraordinary".
"It's a matter for the company and for its board. But you might see in the quite extraordinary reaction on the stock market just how volatile global markets are right now," he says.
"I think it's a bit of a symbol of the of the quite extraordinary volatility unpredictability that we're seeing play out in markets, in the AI sector, but more broadly as well."
Wong defends Bowen after COP talks broke down
Penny Wong is also defending her frontbench colleague Chris Bowen, after talks at the COP summit broke down.
The climate change and energy minister is on his way back to Australia after leaders were unable to reach a consensus despite the drawn-out negotiations.
Wong was the climate minister the last time COP failed to reach an agreement, back in 2009 at the talks in Copenhagen.
She tells ABC's News Breakfast that of course everyone wishes a consensus could've been reached in Türkiye.
"I know what Chris Bowen has done has been to work extremely closely with the Pacific all the way through this process. And to keep faith with them," she says.
"He sought to do that the whole way through, and I'm sure did so in Turkiye as well. And the reason we sought to participate here was because we wanted to keep faith with the Pacific on climate."
AI is already changing how we work and how wars are fought: Wong
Foreign Minister Penny Wong will use a speech to the Senate to warn the rivalry between the US and China is making the world less stable and increasing the risk of conflict.

Wong tells ABC's News Breakfast that Australians can see the way in which the environment is changing and how technology, such as artificial intelligence, is changing how the "great powers are operating".

"An important point is that artificial intelligence is already with us. It's already changing how we work. It's already changing how wars are fought. It's already reshaping our economies and our lives," she says.
"So the question really is, how do you handle that? And as the prime minister said, you have to do it on Australian terms."
So what will the role of middle powers like Australia be? Wong says it's important for us to work with nations like the UK, Canada, the EU and Japan to "secure our position".
Wong reacts to Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang
Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive overnight, just days after the board ruled out his return to the chip maker following revelations of extra-marital affairs.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong is asked by ABC's News Breakfast if she's surprised by that decision.
"It's certainty made news," she says.
"But ultimately [it's] a decision for the board and the company. My focus today is more broadly on … securing Australia's future in a changing world."
Could Labor target EV and home battery subsidies in MYEFO?
As the government looks to make savings in the upcoming mid-year budget update, speculation is rife subsidies for home batteries and electric vehicles could be in its sights.
The cost of the schemes have blown out from initial forecasts in recent years. Labor's Andrew Charlton was asked if the government was considering means testing the subsidies.
"I'm not going to get in front of any announcements that might be might be made, except to say that the treasurer has said that the savings will be substantial," he tells Seven.
Pressed again, Charlton again didn't rule it out.

"Every budget is an opportunity to review government expenditure and making sure it is working for taxpayers. I'm not going to announce any specific measures on this show. We're going to find those out in the next couple of weeks."
That's not a no, hey.
Key Event
Penny Wong will warn US and China are eroding global rules and increasing risk of conflict
Foreign Minister Penny Wong will deliver a major foreign policy speech to parliament today, outlining the ways in which Australia will respond to a changing world.
She will call out the United States and China for making the world less stable, and increasing the risk of conflict.
"The great powers – the United States and China – are competing across every domain, with less regard for the guardrails that once kept competition from tipping into conflict," she will say.
She will argue China is "intensifying" its efforts to "remake the multilateral system" and increasingly militarising disputed issues.
"China is undertaking the largest military build-up by any country since the Second World War, without the transparency and reassurance the region expects," she will say.
Wong will therefore argue the need for middle powers like Australia, India, Indonesia and Japan to deepen their partnerships.
"Amplified middle power diplomacy characterises our approach, bringing together countries that can achieve more in partnership than any one of us could achieve alone," she will say.
Key Event
Albanese to meet with Singaporean counterpart
Wong touched down in Sydney yesterday on the inaugural Singapore Airlines flight to the new Western Sydney airport.
"That's a big plus, and it says something about the importance of the piece of infrastructure that Lawrence Wong will be on that," Albanese said ahead of the PM's arrival yesterday.
The pair caught up on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit but will catch up this morning for breakfast before bilateral talks.
On the agenda for talks is further cooperation under the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership 2.0.
Good morning 👋
Hello friends. Welcome to our politics live blog. I'm Courtney Gould from the ABC's Parliament House team, here to guide you through the day.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong will be out of the blocks early today, ahead of a speech she's giving to the Senate later today. She'll use the address to warn of a new global era of coercion and conflict (more on that shortly).
Expect there to be focus on Treasurer Jim Chalmers after he painted a pretty grim picture of the next year in an economic statement yesterday.

Also on my radar, the status of a couple of key bills the government wants passed this week (digital duty of care, gas reservation scheme ... just to name two). The party's will meet this morning, so it's a bit of a watch this space on if any deals have been reached overnight.
Anyway, enough of me jabbering on. Let's jump straight into the action.
